## Gap Analysis: SOP-CLIN-001 vs. EU AI Act Article 11 (Technical Documentation) & Article 17 (Quality Management System)

### Overview

SOP-CLIN-001 is a well-structured validation SOP that addresses many clinical and technical validation elements. However, when measured against the specific, enumerated requirements of **Article 17(1)(a)–(i)** and **Article 11 / Annex IV (1–9)**, several material gaps emerge. Below is the detailed analysis.

---

## PART 1: GAPS AGAINST ARTICLE 17 — QUALITY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM

Article 17(1) requires the QMS to be "documented in a systematic and orderly manner in the form of written policies, procedures and instructions" and to include **at least** nine enumerated aspects. Here is what's missing from SOP-CLIN-001:

### Art. 17(1)(a) — Regulatory Compliance Strategy
**Requirement:** "A strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for the management of modifications to the high-risk AI system."

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **PARTIAL** | The SOP references "EU AI Act requirements" in Policy Statement 6 and Section 10.2, but there is **no documented regulatory compliance strategy**. Specifically missing: (i) a defined conformity assessment procedure (e.g., which Annex VI/VII/VIII route applies); (ii) procedures for managing modifications to the CDSS — SOP-CLIN-005 is referenced but only as a related document, not integrated; (iii) no mention of the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), CE marking (Article 48), or EU database registration (Article 49). |

### Art. 17(1)(b) — Design Control & Design Verification
**Requirement:** "Techniques, procedures and systematic actions to be used for the design, design control and design verification of the high-risk AI system."

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **GAP** | The SOP covers **validation** (confirming the right product was built) but does not address **design control or design verification** (confirming the product was built right). There are no procedures for: design inputs, design outputs, design reviews, design verification against specifications, or design transfer. The SOP jumps from "Study Design Workshop" (Phase 0) to validation execution. IEC 62304 is listed as a reference but its design control processes are not operationalized. |

### Art. 17(1)(c) — Development, Quality Control & Quality Assurance
**Requirement:** "Techniques, procedures and systematic actions to be used for the development, quality control and quality assurance of the high-risk AI system."

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **GAP** | The SOP does not address the **development** phase at all. It covers validation of the finished model but not: coding standards, code review procedures, unit/integration testing, quality control gates during development, or QA procedures for intermediate development artifacts. SOP-DS-001 is referenced as a related document but its content is not incorporated. |

### Art. 17(1)(d) — Examination, Test and Validation Procedures
**Requirement:** "Examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after the development of the high-risk AI system, and the frequency with which they have to be carried out."

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **PARTIAL** | The SOP covers **post-development validation** thoroughly (Phases 2–5). However, it lacks: (i) testing procedures to be carried out **before** and **during** development (e.g., model unit tests, integration tests, adversarial robustness testing); (ii) explicit **frequency** specifications for re-validation beyond the annual cycle (Section 7.3) — Article 17(1)(d) requires frequency to be specified for each type of test. |

### Art. 17(1)(e) — Technical Specifications
**Requirement:** "Technical specifications, including standards, to be applied and, where the relevant harmonised standards are not applied in full, the means to be used to ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with the requirements set out in Section 2."

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **GAP** | The SOP lists external standards (IEC 62304, ISO 13485, NIST AI RMF) in Section 10.2 but does **not** specify: (i) which technical specifications apply to each CDSS; (ii) which harmonised standards are applied in full vs. partially; (iii) the alternative means used where harmonised standards are not fully applied. This is a core Article 17(1)(e) requirement. |

### Art. 17(1)(f) — Data Management System
**Requirement:** "Systems and procedures for data management, including data acquisition, data collection, data analysis, data labelling, data storage, data filtration, data mining, data aggregation, data retention and any other operation regarding the data that is performed before and for the purposes of the placing on the market or putting into service of high-risk AI systems."

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **PARTIAL** | Section 5.2 covers data curation, de-identification, hold-out set creation, and lockbox procedures. However, missing are: (i) **data labelling** procedures (the GSAG is mentioned but not detailed as a data management procedure); (ii) **data filtration, data mining, and data aggregation** procedures; (iii) **data retention** policies for training/validation/testing data; (iv) procedures for data operations performed **before** the lockbox stage (i.e., during initial model development). |

### Art. 17(1)(g) — Risk Management System
**Requirement:** "The risk management system referred to in Article 9."

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **PARTIAL** | SOP-CLIN-002 (Risk Management and FMEA) is referenced but not integrated. The SOP itself does not operationalize the Article 9 risk management system. Missing: (i) continuous iterative risk management throughout the lifecycle; (ii) identification of reasonably foreseeable **misuse** (not just intended-purpose risks); (iii) evaluation of risks to **fundamental rights** specifically (not just clinical safety); (iv) consideration of adverse impact on persons under 18 and vulnerable groups (Article 9(9)). The FMEA approach is mentioned only in acronyms. |

### Art. 17(1)(h) — Post-Market Monitoring System
**Requirement:** "The post-market monitoring system referred to in Article 72."

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **PARTIAL** | Section 7 covers post-market monitoring with KPIs (PSI, override rate, AEs, fairness). However, Article 72 requires: (i) a **post-market monitoring plan** that is part of the technical documentation (Annex IV); (ii) the plan must follow the Commission's template (due by 2 February 2026); (iii) the system must "actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data" — the SOP mentions a PMCF plan must be "filed within 30 days" but does not specify the **system** itself. The SOP also does not address analysis of interaction with **other AI systems** (Article 72(2)). |

### Art. 17(1)(i) — Incident Reporting & Communication
**Requirement:** "Procedures related to the reporting of a serious incident in accordance with Article 73."

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **GAP** | Section 8.2 covers escalation and mentions "findings are reported to regulatory bodies by the Regulatory Affairs department." However, there is **no specific procedure** for serious incident reporting under Article 73: (i) no defined timeline for reporting serious incidents to market surveillance authorities (Article 73 requires reporting "immediately" and no later than 15 days, or 7 days for widespread infringement); (ii) no procedure for notifying deployers; (iii) no procedure for notifying other providers/importers/distributors. The breach notification language in Section 8.2 references PHI breaches but not AI-specific serious incident reporting. |

### Additional QMS Gaps
- **Resource management** (personnel, infrastructure): The SOP defines roles but does not address how competence, training effectiveness, and resource adequacy are systematically managed as part of the QMS.
- **Accountability framework**: While RACI is defined, there is no documented management responsibility framework for QMS oversight, management review, or QMS performance evaluation.
- **Communication with competent authorities and notified bodies**: No procedure exists for proactive or responsive communication with authorities beyond incident reporting.

---

## PART 2: GAPS AGAINST ARTICLE 11 / ANNEX IV — TECHNICAL DOCUMENTATION

Annex IV requires **nine categories** of information in the technical documentation. The SOP's Final Validation Report (FVR) is described as including "all Annex IV documentation elements" (Section 5.5), but the SOP does not specify what those elements are. Here is what is missing:

### Annex IV §1 — General Description of the AI System
**Requirement:** Intended purpose, provider details, version, interaction with other systems/hardware, instructions for use, deployer information.

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **PARTIAL** | The SOP covers intended purpose (CEDD) and versioning (code freeze). Missing: (i) no requirement to document the **provider's name, address, and contact details** in the technical documentation; (ii) no requirement to document **interaction with other AI systems or hardware/software** (e.g., EHR integration dependencies); (iii) no requirement to document the **instructions for use** as part of the technical documentation package; (iv) no requirement to document the **expected lifetime** and maintenance measures (Article 13(e)). |

### Annex IV §2 — Detailed Description of Elements and Development Process
**Requirement:** Design specifications, algorithms/models, architecture, data requirements, development methodology.

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **GAP** | The SOP focuses on validation outputs, not development process documentation. Missing: (i) **design specifications** for the CDSS; (ii) **architecture diagrams**; (iii) description of **algorithms and models** used; (iv) **development methodology** documentation; (v) description of **data requirements** including Article 10 data governance documentation (data provenance, representativeness, bias examination). |

### Annex IV §3 — Monitoring, Functioning, and Control
**Requirement:** Logging specifications, performance monitoring framework, human oversight mechanisms, control measures.

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **PARTIAL** | Section 7 covers post-deployment monitoring KPIs. Missing: (i) **logging specifications** aligned with Article 12 (automatic recording of events over the system's lifetime); (ii) documentation of **human oversight measures** (Article 14) — the SOP states the CDSS is "an advisory tool" but does not document the specific human oversight mechanisms built into the system; (iii) **control measures** for the CDSS in operation. |

### Annex IV §4 — Performance Metrics
**Requirement:** Description of performance metrics and their appropriateness for the intended purpose.

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **PARTIAL** | Section 5.5 covers performance benchmarks (sensitivity, specificity, lead time, calibration). Missing: (i) explicit justification of **why these metrics are appropriate** for the intended purpose; (ii) **accuracy levels** declared per Article 15(3); (iii) documentation of the **limitations and constraints** of the performance metrics; (iv) **known failure modes** and their clinical implications. |

### Annex IV §5 — Risk Management System Description
**Requirement:** Detailed description of the risk management system.

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **GAP** | The SOP references SOP-CLIN-002 for FMEA but does not require the FVR to include a detailed description of the risk management system. Missing: (i) risk identification and analysis results; (ii) risk evaluation outcomes; (iii) risk management measures adopted; (iv) residual risk assessment; (v) the overall risk-benefit determination. |

### Annex IV §6 — Lifecycle Changes
**Requirement:** Description of changes made to the system throughout its lifecycle.

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **GAP** | The SOP has a Revision History (Section 11) for the SOP itself, but there is **no requirement** in the FVR or technical documentation to track and describe changes made to the **CDSS** throughout its lifecycle. SOP-CLIN-005 (Change Management) is referenced but not integrated. Article 11(1) requires the technical documentation to be "kept up-to-date" — the SOP does not specify a procedure for updating technical documentation when the CDSS is modified. |

### Annex IV §7 — Applied Standards
**Requirement:** List of harmonised standards applied in full or in part.

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **GAP** | Section 10.2 lists external standards but the SOP does not require the FVR to include: (i) a list of which harmonised standards were applied; (ii) which were applied in full vs. in part; (iii) a description of the solutions adopted to meet the requirements where standards were not applied. |

### Annex IV §8 — EU Declaration of Conformity
**Requirement:** Copy of the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47).

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **GAP** | The SOP makes **no mention** of the EU declaration of conformity, its contents, or the requirement to include it in the technical documentation package. |

### Annex IV §9 — Post-Market Monitoring Plan
**Requirement:** The post-market monitoring plan (Article 72(3)).

| Status | Gap |
|---|---|
| **PARTIAL** | Section 7.1 mentions a PMCF plan must be "filed within 30 days of deployment" but does not specify that this plan must be **part of the technical documentation** (as required by Article 72(3)), nor does it specify the plan's required contents per the Commission's implementing act template. |

---

## SUMMARY OF MISSING ELEMENTS

### Critical Gaps (no coverage in SOP):

| # | Gap | Relevant Provision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Design control & design verification procedures** | Art. 17(1)(b) |
| 2 | **Development, quality control & QA procedures** | Art. 17(1)(c) |
| 3 | **Technical specifications with standards gap analysis** | Art. 17(1)(e) |
| 4 | **Serious incident reporting procedure (Article 73)** | Art. 17(1)(i) |
| 5 | **Design specifications & architecture in tech docs** | Annex IV §2 |
| 6 | **Risk management system description in tech docs** | Annex IV §5 |
| 7 | **Lifecycle change documentation for the CDSS** | Annex IV §6 |
| 8 | **List of applied harmonised standards** | Annex IV §7 |
| 9 | **EU declaration of conformity** | Annex IV §8 |
| 10 | **Conformity assessment procedure definition** | Art. 17(1)(a) |
| 11 | **Logging specifications (Article 12)** | Annex IV §3 |
| 12 | **Human oversight mechanism documentation (Article 14)** | Annex IV §3 |

### Partial Gaps (some coverage but incomplete):

## CONCLUSION

SOP-CLIN-001 is fundamentally a **clinical validation procedure**, not a comprehensive Quality Management System or technical documentation framework as required by Articles 17 and 11/Annex IV. The SOP excels at clinical study methodology (lockbox, MRMC, statistical analysis, sign-off gates) but has **no coverage** of design control, development QA, serious incident reporting under Article 73, the EU declaration of conformity, or the structured technical documentation categories required by Annex IV. 

To close these gaps, Meridian would need either: (a) a substantial expansion of SOP-CLIN-001 to encompass the full QMS and technical documentation scope, or (b) a new overarching QMS SOP that integrates SOP-CLIN-001 as the validation module within a broader Article 17-compliant framework, alongside a dedicated Technical Documentation SOP aligned to Annex IV.

**Compliance level: PARTIAL — significant gaps remain.**

## Analysis: SOP-LEGC-005 — Missing GDPR Transparency and Transfer Obligations

Based on a thorough review of SOP-LEGC-005 against the GDPR's transparency obligations (Articles 5, 12, 13, 14, 30, 33, 34) and transfer obligations (Articles 44–49), I have identified the following **specific missing elements**:

---

### A. TRANSPARENCY OBLIGATIONS — MISSING ELEMENTS

#### 1. No Specification of Legal Basis for Processing Personal Data in Regulatory Filings

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 13(1)(c) and Article 14(1)(c) require that data subjects be informed of "the purposes of the processing for which the personal data are intended as well as the legal basis for the processing." When personal data is processed for regulatory filings, the controller must identify whether it relies on Article 6(1)(c) (legal obligation), Article 6(1)(f) (legitimate interest), or another basis.

**What the SOP says:** Policy Statement 6 (Section 4) states only that "Meridian processes the personal data of EU residents in regulatory filings in accordance with GDPR principles" and that "Data subjects are informed about processing activities through Meridian's Privacy Notices posted on the corporate website." There is **no identification of the specific legal basis** relied upon for processing personal data within regulatory filings. The SOP defers entirely to SOP-SECP-012 and website privacy notices without specifying which Article 6 basis applies to regulatory filing processing activities.

**Gap:** The SOP does not require the RFO or any gate reviewer to verify that the legal basis for including personal data in a specific regulatory filing has been identified, documented, and communicated to data subjects.

---

#### 2. No Specification of Categories of Personal Data Processed in Regulatory Filings

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 14(1)(d) (where data is not obtained from the data subject) requires disclosure of "the categories of personal data concerned." Regulatory filings may contain personal data obtained from third-party sources (e.g., clinical data, financial data from partner institutions).

**What the SOP says:** The SOP is silent on categorizing the types of personal data that may appear in regulatory filings. Section 5.2 discusses "Evidence Packages" and data sources but does not require the RFO to identify or document categories of personal data included in the filing.

**Gap:** No requirement to inventory or disclose categories of personal data processed in each regulatory filing.

---

#### 3. No Specification of Retention Periods for Personal Data in Regulatory Filings

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 5(1)(e) (storage limitation) and Article 13(2)(a) / Article 14(2)(a) require that data subjects be informed of "the period for which the personal data will be stored, or if that is not possible, the criteria used to determine that period."

**What the SOP says:** Section 5.5 addresses archival and records management, including WORM-storage compliance archives, but does **not** define a retention period for personal data within regulatory filings, nor does it reference criteria for determining how long personal data in filings will be retained. The archival procedures focus on document integrity and legal holds, not on data minimization or storage limitation for personal data.

**Gap:** No defined retention period or retention criteria for personal data contained in regulatory filings. The WORM-storage archive (AWS S3 Glacier Deep Archive with Compliance Locks) suggests indefinite retention, which may conflict with the storage limitation principle.

---

#### 4. No Mechanism for Data Subject Access to Personal Data Within Regulatory Filings

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 12(2) requires the controller to "facilitate the exercise of data subject rights under Articles 15 to 22." Article 15 provides the right of access. Article 13(2)(b) and 14(2)(c) require informing data subjects of "the existence of the right to request from the controller access to and rectification or erasure of personal data."

**What the SOP says:** The SOP contains **no procedure** for handling a data subject access request (DSAR) that may implicate personal data contained in regulatory filings. There is no mechanism for identifying, extracting, or redacting personal data from filed regulatory documents in response to a DSAR. The "zero-deletion workspace" (Control C-03) and immutable WORM storage may actively conflict with the right to erasure (Article 17) and right to rectification (Article 16).

**Gap:** No DSAR procedure specific to regulatory filings; immutable archival may violate Article 16 (rectification) and Article 17 (erasure) rights.

---

#### 5. No Requirement to Inform Data Subjects of Automated Decision-Making in Regulatory Context

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 13(2)(f) and Article 14(2)(g) require disclosure of "the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, referred to in Article 22(1) and (4) and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences."

**What the SOP says:** The SOP covers SR 11-7 model risk management extensively, including model performance monitoring, validation, and AI incident management. Meridian's Clinical AI Platform and HealthPay Financial Services involve automated processing. However, the SOP does **not** require that data subjects be informed when automated decision-making (including profiling) contributes to regulatory filings that concern them.

**Gap:** No transparency requirement regarding automated decision-making or profiling in the context of regulatory filings.

---

#### 6. No Right to Object or Right to Withdraw Consent Procedures for Regulatory Filing Data

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 13(2)(b) and (c) require informing data subjects of the right to object (Article 21) and, where consent is the legal basis, the right to withdraw consent (Article 7(3)).

**What the SOP says:** The SOP does not address how a data subject's objection to processing or withdrawal of consent would be handled if their personal data is already incorporated into a regulatory filing. There is no procedure for assessing whether an objection should halt or modify a pending regulatory submission.

**Gap:** No procedure for handling objections or consent withdrawals that intersect with regulatory filing obligations.

---

#### 7. No Source Disclosure for Personal Data Not Obtained from the Data Subject

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 14(2)(f) requires disclosure of "from which source the personal data originate, and if applicable, whether it came from publicly accessible sources."

**What the SOP says:** Section 5.2 discusses "Evidence Packages" and data sources for quantitative models, but does not require the RFO to document or disclose the source of personal data when it was not collected directly from the data subject (e.g., clinical data from healthcare providers, financial data from partner institutions).

**Gap:** No requirement to document or disclose the origin of personal data included in regulatory filings when obtained from third parties.

---

#### 8. No Timely Provision of Article 14 Information (Within One Month)

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 14(3)(a) requires that where personal data has not been obtained from the data subject, the controller shall provide the information "within a reasonable period after obtaining the personal data, but at the latest within one month."

**What the SOP says:** The SOP's 60-day drafting window (Section 5.2) and gated review workflow (Section 5.3) do not incorporate any check or trigger to ensure that Article 14 information has been provided to data subjects within the one-month deadline when personal data is sourced from third parties for inclusion in a filing.

**Gap:** No procedural trigger to ensure Article 14 transparency information is provided within the statutory one-month deadline.

---

#### 9. No Granular Privacy Notice Specific to Regulatory Filing Processing

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 12(1) requires information to be provided "in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language." The EDPB has emphasized that generic privacy notices are insufficient where specific, high-risk processing activities occur.

**What the SOP says:** Policy Statement 6 references only "Meridian's Privacy Notices posted on the corporate website." There is no requirement for a layered or specific privacy notice addressing the particular processing activities involved in regulatory filings (which may involve health data, financial data, and AI-related inferences about data subjects).

**Gap:** Reliance on generic website privacy notices without a requirement for specific, contextual transparency about regulatory filing processing activities.

---

### B. TRANSFER OBLIGATIONS — MISSING ELEMENTS

#### 10. No Identification of Specific Transfer Safeguard Mechanism

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 13(1)(f) and Article 14(1)(f) require that where personal data is transferred to a third country, the controller must inform data subjects of "the existence or absence of an adequacy decision by the Commission, or in the case of transfers referred to in Article 46 or 47, or the second subparagraph of Article 49(1), reference to the appropriate or suitable safeguards and the means by which to obtain a copy of them or where they have been made available."

**What the SOP says:** Policy Statement 6 states: "When personal data is transferred from the EU to Meridian's US-based analytics teams for a regulatory submission, Meridian ensures appropriate safeguards are in place." This is **vague and non-specific**. It does not identify:
- Whether the US is covered by an adequacy decision (the EU-US Data Privacy Framework);
- Whether Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) are used (Article 46(2)(c));
- Whether Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) are in place (Article 47);
- Whether a Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) has been conducted (as required post-*Schrems II*);
- The means by which data subjects can obtain a copy of the safeguards.

**Gap:** The SOP fails to specify which transfer mechanism is relied upon, fails to reference the EU-US Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision, and fails to inform data subjects how to obtain a copy of the safeguards — all required by Articles 13(1)(f) and 14(1)(f).

---

#### 11. No Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) Requirement

**GDP Requirement (as interpreted by CJEU in *Schrems II*, C-311/18):** Before transferring personal data to a third country under Article 46 safeguards, the controller must conduct a Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) to evaluate whether the law and practice of the third country ensure a level of protection essentially equivalent to that guaranteed in the EU.

**What the SOP says:** The SOP contains no requirement for a TIA before personal data is transferred to US-based analytics teams for regulatory submissions. The Evidence Package compilation (Section 5.2) and review gates (Section 5.3) do not include a TIA checkpoint.

**Gap:** No TIA requirement before EU-to-US personal data transfers for regulatory filing purposes.

---

#### 12. No Onward Transfer Restrictions or Documentation

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 44 requires that "all provisions in this Chapter [V] shall be applied in order to ensure that the level of protection of natural persons guaranteed by this Regulation is not undermined." Article 46 safeguards must address onward transfers.

**What the SOP says:** The SOP does not address whether personal data in regulatory filings, once submitted to a regulator (e.g., FDA, EU supervisory authorities), may be further transferred by that regulator to other third parties. There is no documentation of onward transfer risk assessment or contractual restrictions with regulators regarding their handling of personal data contained in filings.

**Gap:** No assessment or documentation of onward transfer risks once personal data is disclosed to regulatory addressees.

---

#### 13. No Article 49 Derogation Documentation (If Applicable)

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 49(1) permits transfers under specific derogations (e.g., important reasons of public interest, establishment/exercise/defense of legal claims). Article 49(2) requires that where a transfer relies on the "compelling legitimate interests" derogation, the controller must inform the supervisory authority and the data subject.

**What the SOP says:** The SOP does not address whether any EU-to-US transfers for regulatory filings rely on Article 49 derogations. If SCCs/BCRs are not in place for a particular transfer, the SOP provides no mechanism to document reliance on a derogation or to notify the supervisory authority as required by Article 49(2).

**Gap:** No procedure for documenting or notifying reliance on Article 49 derogations.

---

### C. CROSS-CUTTING / ACCOUNTABILITY GAPS

#### 14. No Article 30 ROPA Integration for Regulatory Filing Processing Activities

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 30(1) requires controllers to maintain a Record of Processing Activities including: name and contact details of the controller and DPO; purposes of processing; categories of data subjects and personal data; categories of recipients (including third country recipients); transfers to third countries and documentation of safeguards; and "where possible, the envisaged time limits for erasure of the different categories of data."

**What the SOP says:** Section 3.1 mentions the DPO (Dr. Klaus Weber) as RFO for "Records of Processing Activities (ROPA) summaries when requested by an SA." However, the SOP does **not** require that the processing of personal data within each regulatory filing be recorded as a distinct processing activity in Meridian's ROPA, nor does it require the RFO to provide the necessary metadata (categories of data, retention periods, transfer safeguards) to the DPO for ROPA inclusion.

**Gap:** No procedural integration between the regulatory filing workflow and the ROPA maintenance obligation.

---

#### 15. No DPIA Trigger for High-Risk Regulatory Filings Containing Personal Data

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 35(1) requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where processing "is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons." Given that Meridian processes health data (special category data under Article 9) through its Clinical AI Platform and financial data through HealthPay, regulatory filings containing such data likely trigger the DPIA requirement.

**What the SOP says:** The SOP contains no DPIA trigger or checkpoint. The G1-G5 review gates do not include a DPIA assessment. The Materiality flag (Section 5.3) is based on compliance gap admissions and safety signals — not on data protection risk.

**Gap:** No DPIA requirement for regulatory filings that involve large-scale processing of special category data or systematic evaluation of data subjects.

---

#### 16. No Article 36 Prior Consultation Procedure

**GDPR Requirement:** Article 36(1) requires the controller to "consult the supervisory authority prior to processing where a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 indicates that the processing would result in a high risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk."

**What the SOP says:** Section 3.1 references the DPO's role in "consultation notifications under Article 36," but the SOP's detailed procedures (Section 5) contain **no workflow step** that triggers an Article 36 consultation when a regulatory filing involves high-risk personal data processing. There is no gate or checkpoint for this.

**Gap:** No procedural integration of Article 36 prior consultation into the regulatory filing workflow.

---

### SUMMARY TABLE OF MISSING ELEMENTS

| # | Missing Element | GDPR Article(s) | Category |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Legal basis identification for personal data in filings | Art. 13(1)(c), 14(1)(c) | Transparency |
| 2 | Categories of personal data in regulatory filings | Art. 14(1)(d) | Transparency |
| 3 | Retention periods / criteria for personal data in filings | Art. 5(1)(e), 13(2)(a), 14(2)(a) | Transparency |
| 4 | DSAR procedure for personal data in regulatory filings | Art. 12(2), 15, 16, 17 | Transparency |
| 5 | Automated decision-making disclosure in filing context | Art. 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g), 22 | Transparency |
| 6 | Objection / consent withdrawal procedure for filing data | Art. 13(2)(b)-(c), 21, 7(3) | Transparency |
| 7 | Source disclosure for third-party personal data | Art. 14(2)(f) | Transparency |
| 8 | Article 14 one-month information deadline trigger | Art. 14(3)(a) | Transparency |
| 9 | Specific privacy notice for regulatory filing processing | Art. 12(1) | Transparency |
| 10 | Specific transfer safeguard mechanism identification | Art. 13(1)(f), 14(1)(f), 44-46 | Transfer |
| 11 | Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) requirement | Art. 44, 46 (*Schrems II*) | Transfer |
| 12 | Onward transfer restrictions / risk documentation | Art. 44 | Transfer |
| 13 | Article 49 derogation documentation procedure | Art. 49 | Transfer |
| 14 | ROPA integration for regulatory filing processing | Art. 30 | Accountability |
| 15 | DPIA trigger for high-risk filing-related processing | Art. 35 | Accountability |
| 16 | Article 36 prior consultation workflow integration | Art. 36 | Accountability |

---

### CONCLUSION

SOP-LEGC-005 is a well-structured regulatory filing procedure with strong governance for SR 11-7, EU MDR, and AI Act obligations. However, its treatment of GDPR is **superficial and largely deferential** — Policy Statement 6 (Section 4) is a single paragraph that gestures toward GDPR compliance without operationalizing it. The SOP treats GDPR as a background compliance framework rather than integrating its specific transparency and transfer obligations into the filing workflow. The 16 missing elements identified above represent concrete, actionable gaps that expose Meridian to risk of GDPR non-compliance, particularly given the sensitivity of the health and financial data processed through its Clinical AI and HealthPay platforms.

**Compliance level: PARTIAL — SIGNIFICANT GAPS**

## Gap Analysis: SOP-ITOP-005 vs. SOC 2 CC7 (System Operations / Monitoring) and CC8 (Change Management)

Based on a detailed review of SOP-ITOP-005 (v4.7, 2025-12-15) against the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria CC7 and CC8 points of focus, I have identified the following **missing or insufficiently addressed controls**:

---

### CC7.1 — Detection and Monitoring Procedures (Configuration Vulnerabilities)

| Point of Focus | Status | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| **Uses Defined Configuration Standards** | **MISSING** | The SOP references baselines for *performance* metrics (CPU, memory, latency, etc.) but does not define or reference **security configuration hardening standards** (e.g., CIS benchmarks, AWS Security Hub rules, or internal golden AMI standards). CC7.1 explicitly requires defined configuration standards for hardening systems. |
| **Implements Change-Detection Mechanisms** | **MISSING** | CC7.1 requires "a change-detection mechanism (for example, file integrity monitoring tools) to alert personnel to unauthorized modifications of critical system files, configuration files, or content files." The SOP is silent on file integrity monitoring (FIM) or any equivalent change-detection tooling. Datadog monitors performance metrics but does not appear to cover unauthorized file/config changes. |
| **Detects Unknown or Unauthorized Components** | **MISSING** | No procedure exists to detect the introduction of unknown or unauthorized components (e.g., rogue EC2 instances, unauthorized containers, unapproved software). The SOP's monitoring is scoped to known, in-scope resources only. |
| **Conducts Vulnerability Scans** | **MISSING** | CC7.1 requires vulnerability scans "on a periodic basis and after significant changes are made to the environment." The SOP does not mention vulnerability scanning at all — neither scheduled scans nor event-driven scans triggered by capacity changes. |

---

### CC7.2 — Anomaly Monitoring

| Point of Focus | Status | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| **Implements Detection Policies, Procedures, and Tools** | **PARTIAL** | The SOP has strong performance anomaly detection (Tier 1–3 thresholds, synthetic checks, dead man's switch). However, CC7.2 also requires detection for "potential intrusions, inappropriate access, and anomalies in the operation of or unusual activity on systems" — including use of threat intelligence sources. The SOP's monitoring is exclusively performance/capacity-oriented; security anomaly detection (e.g., unusual API call patterns, unauthorized access attempts) is not addressed. |
| **Designs Detection Measures** | **PARTIAL** | CC7.2 calls for detection measures covering: (1) compromise of physical barriers, (2) unauthorized actions of authorized personnel, (3) compromised credentials, (4) unauthorized external access, (5) compromise of external parties, and (6) unauthorized hardware/software. The SOP addresses none of these security detection dimensions. |
| **Monitors Detection Tools for Effective Operation** | **MISSING** | CC7.2 requires processes to "monitor and maintain the effectiveness of detection tools." The SOP does not include any procedure for validating that Datadog monitors, synthetic checks, or alerting pipelines themselves are functioning correctly (e.g., monitor health checks, alert pipeline testing). |

---

### CC7.3 — Security Event Evaluation

| Point of Focus | Status | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| **Responds to Security Incidents / Evaluates Effectiveness Periodically** | **PARTIAL** | The SOP references SOP-ISEC-002 for incident response and includes Post-Incident Reviews (PIRs) for capacity incidents. However, CC7.3 requires periodic evaluation of the *effectiveness* of incident response policies and procedures. The SOP itself acknowledges this gap explicitly in §4.5: *"Although an incident response plan has been documented to address capacity-driven outages, regular tabletop exercises to rehearse response procedures are not currently scheduled."* This is a **self-identified gap**. |

---

### CC7.4 — Incident Response Execution

| Point of Focus | Status | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| **Evaluates the Effectiveness of Incident Response** | **MISSING** | CC7.4 explicitly requires: "The design of incident-response activities is evaluated for effectiveness on a periodic basis." No tabletop exercises, simulation drills, or IR plan testing are scheduled per §4.5. |
| **Periodically Evaluates Incidents** | **PARTIAL** | The SOP requires PIRs within 5 business days of P1/P2 capacity incidents (§5.5), which is good. However, CC7.4 also requires periodic *aggregate* review of incidents to identify patterns and root causes for systemic changes. The SOP lacks a scheduled (e.g., quarterly) trend analysis of all capacity incidents. |

---

### CC7.5 — Incident Recovery

| Point of Focus | Status | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| **Implements Incident-Recovery Plan Testing** | **MISSING** | CC7.5 requires: "Incident-recovery plan testing is performed on a periodic basis. The testing includes (1) development of testing scenarios based on threat likelihood and magnitude; (2) consideration of relevant system components from across the entity that can impair availability; (3) scenarios that consider the potential for the lack of availability of key personnel; and (4) revision of resilience posture and continuity plans based on test results." The SOP has no recovery plan testing whatsoever — no tabletop exercises, no failover drills, no disaster recovery testing procedures. |
| **Improves Response and Recovery Procedures** | **PARTIAL** | While PIRs produce Jira action items (§5.5), there is no formal feedback loop to update the incident response *plan* or recovery *procedures* based on lessons learned. |

---

### CC8.1 — Change Management

| Point of Focus | Status | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| **Manages Changes Throughout the System Life Cycle** | **PARTIAL** | The SOP's change management integration (§4.4, §5.4) is strong for *infrastructure capacity changes* (IaC PR workflow, ServiceNow CHG, segregation of duties). However, the scope is limited to "changes to production infrastructure that alters compute, memory, storage, or network capacity." CC8.1 applies to *all* system changes — infrastructure, data, software, and procedures. Changes to monitoring thresholds, alert configurations, runbooks, and procedural documents are not covered by the formal change process. |
| **Designs and Develops Changes** | **MISSING** | CC8.1 requires: "A process is in place to design and develop system changes in a secure manner." The SOP describes *how to execute* scaling changes but does not address secure design/development practices for changes (e.g., security review of Terraform plans, threat modeling for architectural changes). |
| **Documents Changes** | **PARTIAL** | The IaC workflow documents changes via Git history and ServiceNow tickets. However, CC8.1 requires documentation "to support ongoing maintenance of the system and to support internal and external users in performing their responsibilities." There is no requirement in the SOP to update runbooks, architecture diagrams, or the CMDB after capacity changes are implemented. |
| **Tests Changes** | **MISSING** | CC8.1 explicitly requires a process to **test** changes. The SOP's scaling runbooks (§5.4.1, §5.4.2) include validation steps (e.g., confirming ALB healthy host count) but do not include pre-implementation testing in a staging/UAT environment. For vertical scaling of stateful services, there is no mention of testing the change in a non-production environment before production execution. |
| **Manages Patch Changes** | **MISSING** | CC8.1 requires: "A process is in place to identify, evaluate, test, approve, and implement patches in a timely manner on infrastructure and software." The SOP is entirely silent on patch management — no mention of OS patching, dependency updates, or security patch deployment procedures. |
| **Considers System Resilience (Availability)** | **PARTIAL** | CC8.1's availability point of focus requires that "the entity considers system resilience when designing its systems and tests resilience during development." The SOP addresses resilience through scaling and DR environment provisioning but does not include resilience *testing* (e.g., chaos engineering, failure injection, or controlled disruption testing). |
| **Emergency Change Process** | **PARTIAL** | §8.1 acknowledges emergency security patches as an exception scenario, and §8.3 allows the CTO to "override standard change management lead times for critical fixes." However, there is no defined **emergency change procedure** with post-hoc review requirements. CC8.1 expects all changes — including emergency ones — to be authorized, documented, and reviewed. The exception process (§8.2) requires risk assessment within 1 business day, which may be too slow for an emergency change that has already been deployed. |

---

## Summary of Missing Controls

### HIGH SEVERITY (likely to result in audit findings):

1. **No vulnerability scanning** — CC7.1 requires periodic scans and post-change scans. Completely absent.
2. **No file integrity monitoring / change-detection mechanisms** — CC7.1 requires FIM or equivalent. Absent.
3. **No incident response or recovery plan testing** — CC7.4 and CC7.5 require periodic testing (tabletop exercises, recovery drills). The SOP itself acknowledges this gap (§4.5).
4. **No pre-implementation testing of changes** — CC8.1 requires testing changes before production. The scaling runbooks skip staging validation.
5. **No patch management process** — CC8.1 requires a formal patch identification, evaluation, testing, approval, and implementation process. Absent.

### MEDIUM SEVERITY (partial coverage, needs strengthening):

6. **No security configuration hardening standards** — CC7.1 requires defined configuration standards. Only performance baselines exist.
7. **No detection of unknown/unauthorized components** — CC7.1 requires procedures to detect rogue assets.
8. **Monitoring scope is exclusively performance-based** — CC7.2 requires security anomaly detection (intrusions, unauthorized access, credential compromise). Not addressed.
9. **No monitoring-tool health checks** — CC7.2 requires validating that detection tools themselves are operational.
10. **No aggregate incident trend analysis** — CC7.4 requires periodic review of incident patterns beyond individual PIRs.
11. **Change documentation does not extend to procedural/configuration changes** — CC8.1 scope is broader than infrastructure capacity changes.
12. **No secure design review for changes** — CC8.1 requires changes to be designed and developed securely.
13. **No formal emergency change procedure with mandatory post-hoc review** — CC8.1 expects all changes to be authorized and documented.
14. **No resilience testing** — CC8.1 (availability) requires testing system resilience during development.

---

**Compliance level:** SOP-ITOP-005 is **strong on capacity-specific operational controls** (monitoring thresholds, IaC-based scaling, segregation of duties, cost safeguards) but has **significant gaps in security monitoring integration, vulnerability management, change testing, patch management, and incident response/recovery testing**. These gaps span both CC7 and CC8 and would likely result in multiple findings during a SOC 2 Type 2 examination.

## Gap Analysis: SOP-LEGC-005 vs. HIPAA Breach-Reporting and De-Identification Requirements

After a thorough review of SOP-LEGC-005 (Regulatory Filing and Reporting) against the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR §§ 164.400–164.414) and the HIPAA De-Identification Standard (45 CFR § 164.514), I have identified the following **specific missing elements**:

---

### A. BREACH-REPORTING GAPS

#### 1. No Breach Risk Assessment Procedure (45 CFR § 164.402(2))

The SOP is entirely silent on the **four-factor risk assessment** that HIPAA requires whenever an impermissible use or disclosure of PHI occurs. Under § 164.402(2), an impermissible acquisition, access, use, or disclosure of PHI is **presumed to be a breach** unless the covered entity demonstrates a "low probability that the PHI has been compromised" based on a documented risk assessment of at least:

| Factor | Required Analysis |
|---|---|
| **(i)** | The nature and extent of the PHI involved (types of identifiers, likelihood of re-identification) |
| **(ii)** | The unauthorized person who used the PHI or to whom the disclosure was made |
| **(iii)** | Whether the PHI was actually acquired or viewed |
| **(iv)** | The extent to which the risk to the PHI has been mitigated |

**SOP-LEGC-005 has no mention of this risk assessment whatsoever.** The SOP's incident classification (C-07) is limited to "Serious Incident" under EU MDR / AI Act criteria and does not incorporate the HIPAA breach-presumption framework. This is a critical gap: without this assessment, Meridian cannot lawfully determine whether a given incident triggers notification obligations.

---

#### 2. No Individual Notification Procedure (45 CFR § 164.404)

The SOP contains **zero provisions** for notifying affected individuals following a breach of unsecured PHI. HIPAA § 164.404 requires:

- **Timing:** Notification "without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery" (§ 164.404(b)).
- **Content:** A specific five-element notice including: (A) description of what happened and dates; (B) types of PHI involved; (C) steps individuals should take to protect themselves; (D) what the covered entity is doing to investigate, mitigate, and prevent further breaches; and (E) contact procedures including a toll-free number, email, website, or postal address (§ 164.404(c)(1)).
- **Plain language requirement** (§ 164.404(c)(2)).
- **Method:** First-class mail (or email with consent), substitute notice when contact info is insufficient (including conspicuous website posting for 90 days and a toll-free number active for 90 days when 10+ individuals lack valid addresses), and additional notice in urgent situations (§ 164.404(d)).
- **Deceased individuals:** Notification to next of kin or personal representative (§ 164.404(d)(1)(ii)).

**None of these requirements appear in SOP-LEGC-005.**

---

#### 3. No Media Notification Procedure (45 CFR § 164.406)

For breaches involving **more than 500 residents of a State or jurisdiction**, HIPAA requires notification to "prominent media outlets serving the State or jurisdiction" within 60 days (§ 164.406). The SOP is silent on this obligation.

---

#### 4. No HHS Secretary Notification Procedure (45 CFR § 164.408)

HIPAA requires covered entities to notify the Secretary of HHS:

- **500+ individuals:** Contemporaneously with individual notice, via the HHS breach portal (§ 164.408(b)).
- **Fewer than 500 individuals:** Maintain a log and submit annually no later than 60 days after the end of each calendar year (§ 164.408(c)).

The SOP's Filing Calendar (Section 5.1) and report types (Section 1.2) do not reference HHS breach notifications at all. The "Regulatory Addressee" role in the RACI matrix does not contemplate HHS OCR as a recipient.

---

#### 5. No Business Associate Breach Notification Workflow (45 CFR § 164.410)

HIPAA § 164.410 requires business associates to notify the covered entity of a breach within 60 days, including identification of each affected individual and all information the covered entity needs to fulfill its own notification duties. The SOP defines "BA" in the glossary but contains **no procedure** for:

- Receiving and triaging BA breach notifications
- Ensuring BA notifications include the required content (individual identification, § 164.410(c)(1))
- The covered entity's own clock starting upon BA notification

---

#### 6. No Law Enforcement Delay Provision (45 CFR § 164.412)

HIPAA § 164.412 permits delaying notification if a law enforcement official states it would impede a criminal investigation or damage national security. The SOP's exception handling (Section 8) covers extension requests but does not address this specific HIPAA carve-out.

---

#### 7. No Burden of Proof Documentation (45 CFR § 164.414(b))

HIPAA § 164.414(b) places the burden of proof on the covered entity or business associate to demonstrate that all notifications were made or that the use/disclosure did not constitute a breach. While the SOP has an Evidence Package (Section 5.2.3) and archival procedures (Section 5.5), there is **no specific requirement** to maintain documentation sufficient to meet this burden of proof for breach determinations — including the four-factor risk assessment documentation, notification records, and proof of delivery.

---

#### 8. No Breach-Specific Administrative Requirements (45 CFR § 164.414(a))

HIPAA § 164.414(a) cross-references the administrative requirements of § 164.530(b), (d), (e), (g), (h), (i), and (j) — covering training, complaints, sanctions, mitigation, whistleblower protections, policies/procedures, and documentation. While the SOP has training (Section 9) and whistleblower provisions (Section 8.3), it does not tie these specifically to breach notification compliance as HIPAA requires.

---

### B. DE-IDENTIFICATION GAPS

#### 9. No De-Identification Procedure at All (45 CFR § 164.514(a)–(b))

The SOP is **completely silent** on de-identification of PHI. HIPAA § 164.514(b) provides two mutually exclusive paths:

| Method | Requirements |
|---|---|
| **Expert Determination** (§ 164.514(b)(1)) | A qualified person applies statistical/scientific principles, determines the risk is "very small" that information could identify an individual, and **documents the methods and results** of that analysis. |
| **Safe Harbor** (§ 164.514(b)(2)) | Removal of **18 specific identifiers** (names, geographic subdivisions smaller than a state, dates directly related to an individual, telephone numbers, fax numbers, email addresses, SSNs, medical record numbers, health plan beneficiary numbers, account numbers, certificate/license numbers, vehicle identifiers/serial numbers, device identifiers/serial numbers, URLs, IP addresses, biometric identifiers including finger/voice prints, full-face photographic images and comparable images, and any other unique identifying number/characteristic/code) **AND** the covered entity has no actual knowledge that the information could be used alone or in combination to identify the individual. |

**Neither method is referenced, operationalized, or governed by SOP-LEGC-005.** This is a material gap given that Meridian's scope includes "Clinical AI Platform" and "MedInsight Analytics" — business units that almost certainly handle PHI and may need to de-identify data for research, analytics, or reporting purposes.

---

#### 10. No Re-Identification Prohibition or Controls (45 CFR § 164.502(d)(2))

HIPAA § 164.502(d)(2) provides that disclosure of a code or means of re-identification constitutes disclosure of PHI, and that re-identified information must be treated as PHI again. The SOP contains no controls around re-identification codes, no prohibition on re-identification without authorization, and no procedure for handling re-identified data.

---

### C. STRUCTURAL / GOVERNANCE GAPS

#### 11. No HIPAA Privacy Official or Breach-Specific RFO

HIPAA § 164.530(a)(1) requires designation of a privacy official. While the SOP names a CPO/DPO (Dr. Klaus Weber), his defined role is limited to GDPR submissions. There is **no designated HIPAA Privacy Official** with specific responsibility for breach determination, risk assessment, and notification execution. The "Security Incident Response Lead" (Deputy CISO) is designated for "state breach notification laws and EU AI Act critical incident reporting" — but HIPAA breach notification is conspicuously absent from this role description.

---

#### 12. No Breach-Specific Training Module

The SOP's training modules (MGT-110, MGT-210, MGT-310) cover regulatory filing generally, SR 11-7 governance, and duty of candor — but **none** covers HIPAA breach determination, the four-factor risk assessment, notification timelines, or de-identification requirements.

---

### SUMMARY TABLE OF MISSING ELEMENTS

| # | Missing Element | HIPAA Citation | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Four-factor breach risk assessment | § 164.402(2) | **Critical** |
| 2 | Individual notification procedure (timing, content, method, plain language, substitute notice, deceased individuals) | § 164.404 | **Critical** |
| 3 | Media notification for 500+ residents per State | § 164.406 | **High** |
| 4 | HHS Secretary notification (500+ contemporaneous; <500 annual log) | § 164.408 | **Critical** |
| 5 | Business Associate breach notification workflow | § 164.410 | **High** |
| 6 | Law enforcement delay provision | § 164.412 | **Medium** |
| 7 | Burden of proof documentation for breach determinations | § 164.414(b) | **High** |
| 8 | Breach-specific administrative requirements linkage | § 164.414(a) | **Medium** |
| 9 | De-identification procedure (Expert Determination or Safe Harbor) | § 164.514(b) | **Critical** |
| 10 | Re-identification controls and prohibition | § 164.502(d)(2) | **Medium** |
| 11 | Designated HIPAA Privacy Official with breach responsibility | § 164.530(a)(1) | **High** |
| 12 | HIPAA breach-specific training module | § 164.530(b) | **High** |

---

### CONCLUSION

SOP-LEGC-005 is a well-structured regulatory filing SOP — but it was clearly designed around financial services (SR 11-7), medical device (EU MDR), and AI governance (EU AI Act) frameworks. **HIPAA breach notification and de-identification are essentially absent from the document.** The SOP's scope statement (Section 1.2) lists HIPAA as a covered regime, but the detailed procedures, RACI matrix, Filing Calendar, controls, KPIs, and training modules contain no operationalization of HIPAA's breach-reporting or de-identification requirements. This represents a significant compliance exposure for Meridian Health Technologies as a HIPAA covered entity.

**Compliance level: SOP-LEGC-005 does not meet HIPAA breach-reporting or de-identification requirements.**

I now have a thorough understanding of both the SOP and SR 11-7 requirements. Let me compile the gap analysis.

---

## Gap Analysis: SOP-AIML-006 vs. SR 11-7 Ongoing Monitoring Expectations

Based on a detailed comparison of SOP-AIML-006 (Model Performance Monitoring, v4.4) against SR 11-7's ongoing monitoring requirements, the following **specific elements are MISSING**:

---

### 1. **Process Verification (Complete Gap)**

SR 11-7 explicitly requires ongoing monitoring to include **process verification** — confirming that models are being used as intended, that inputs are correctly specified, and that outputs are accurately transmitted to downstream systems (SR 11-7, Section V). The SOP contains no dedicated process verification procedure. While Section 5.2 covers performance metrics and Section 5.3 covers drift, there is no mechanism to verify that:

- Model inputs remain correctly specified and aligned with the model's design
- Outputs are accurately transmitted to downstream systems without corruption
- The model's scope of use has not been informally extended beyond its validated application

The SOP defers data quality monitoring entirely to SOP-DE-008 (Section 1.3), but SR 11-7 places this squarely within the ongoing monitoring function itself.

---

### 2. **Benchmarking Against Independent Alternatives (Complete Gap)**

SR 11-7's ongoing monitoring pillar explicitly requires **benchmarking** — comparing model outputs against an independent alternative such as a challenger model, a simplified rule-based approach, or a prior model generation. The SOP mentions "Champion-Challenger" in Section 2 (Definitions) but explicitly states: *"a formal Challenger Model governance policy for high-impact decisions is not currently in scope of this SOP."* There is no requirement to:

- Maintain an independent benchmark or challenger model for comparison
- Periodically compare production model outputs against an alternative methodology
- Document the rationale for the chosen benchmark (or its absence)

This is a material gap under SR 11-7's three-pillar validation framework.

---

### 3. **Outcomes Analysis / Back-Testing as a Distinct Monitoring Activity (Partial Gap)**

SR 11-7 identifies **outcomes analysis** (including back-testing) as a distinct, standalone monitoring activity separate from routine metric tracking. While the SOP addresses ground-truth-linked metrics (Section 5.2.1) and delayed-label pipelines (Section 5.2.2), it does not establish:

- A formal, periodic **back-testing** cadence comparing predictions to actual outcomes over defined historical periods
- **Outlier analysis** as a distinct monitoring procedure (SR 11-7 specifically calls this out)
- A requirement for the independent validation function to review outcomes analysis results

The SOP's approach is continuous/automated but lacks the structured, periodic back-testing review that SR 11-7 contemplates.

---

### 4. **Active Monitoring of Data Input Changes (Complete Gap)**

Per SR 11-7 and interpretive guidance (Grant Thornton, 2023), ongoing monitoring must include **active monitoring of data changes** — tracking changes in data type, vendor, and repositories for both internal and external data inputs. The SOP:

- References SOP-DE-008 for data quality but does not incorporate data input change tracking into the monitoring framework
- Has no procedure for verifying that external data sources remain consistent with model purpose and design
- Lacks documentation requirements for data source changes as part of governance

---

### 5. **Model Limitations Assessment as Part of Ongoing Monitoring (Complete Gap)**

SR 11-7 states: *"An effective ongoing monitoring plan may also include regularly assessing any model limitations at the development stage and over time."* The SOP contains no requirement to:

- Periodically reassess model limitations identified during development
- Document whether those limitations have changed in severity or nature
- Link limitation assessments to monitoring findings

---

### 6. **Aggregate Model Risk Monitoring (Complete Gap)**

SR 11-7 explicitly requires assessing model risk **in aggregate**: *"Sound practice involves assessing model risk both individually and in aggregate. Aggregate risk reflects interactions and dependencies among models; reliance on common assumptions, data, or methodologies; and any other factors that could adversely affect several models and their outputs simultaneously."*

The SOP monitors models individually (per-model dashboards, per-model alerts). There is **no mechanism** for:

- Monitoring cross-model dependencies or common failure modes
- Identifying that multiple models rely on the same data pipeline or assumption set
- Aggregating model risk across the portfolio for reporting purposes

---

### 7. **Board and Senior Management Reporting on Model Risk (Significant Gap)**

SR 11-7 requires: *"Senior management, directly and through relevant committees, is responsible for regularly reporting to the board on significant model risk, from individual models and in the aggregate, and on compliance with policy."*

The SOP's reporting cadence (Section 7.2) includes an Executive Summary to the Chief AI Officer, CMO, and CFO on a **quarterly** basis, but:

- There is no explicit **board-level** reporting requirement
- The Executive Summary is described as covering "aggregate program health" but does not explicitly address **aggregate model risk** as SR 11-7 defines it
- There is no requirement for reporting on **compliance with model risk management policy** to the board

---

### 8. **Independent Validation Integration with Ongoing Monitoring (Structural Gap)**

SR 11-7 requires that validation be performed by personnel **independent from model development**, with organizational separation. The SOP's monitoring is entirely operated by the MLOps team (which sits within AI/ML Engineering — the same organization that develops models). There is no:

- Defined handoff or integration point where independent validators review monitoring outputs
- Requirement for independent validation sign-off on monitoring thresholds or procedures
- Evidence of "effective challenge" in the monitoring design or execution

The SOP's governance (Section 6.4) restricts alert threshold changes to MLOps and the Director of AI/ML Engineering — both on the development side, creating a structural conflict with SR 11-7's independence expectations.

---

### 9. **Model Inventory Integration with Monitoring (Gap)**

SR 11-7 expects a **complete model inventory** with each model's name, owner, purpose, risk tier, last validation date, and validation status — integrated with ongoing monitoring. While the SOP references the Model Registry (MLflow) in Section 5.1, it does not require:

- Risk tiering of models that drives differentiated monitoring intensity
- Tracking of last validation date as part of the monitoring dashboard
- Monitoring status linked to the model's validation status

---

### 10. **Formal Change Control for Monitoring Thresholds (Partial Gap)**

SR 11-7 emphasizes governance and controls. While Section 6.4 restricts write access to alerting thresholds, there is no:

- Formal change control process for modifying monitoring thresholds
- Requirement for independent review/approval of threshold changes
- Documentation trail linking threshold changes to justification and approval

---

### Summary Table

| # | Missing Element | SR 11-7 Reference | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Process Verification | Section V — Ongoing Monitoring | **High** |
| 2 | Benchmarking Against Independent Alternatives | Section V — Pillar 2 | **High** |
| 3 | Formal Back-Testing / Outlier Analysis as Distinct Activity | Section V — Outcomes Analysis | **Medium** |
| 4 | Active Data Input Change Tracking | Section V — Ongoing Monitoring (Inputs) | **High** |
| 5 | Periodic Model Limitations Reassessment | Section V — Ongoing Monitoring Plan | **Medium** |
| 6 | Aggregate Model Risk Monitoring | Section III — Overview | **High** |
| 7 | Board-Level Reporting on Model Risk | Section VI — Governance | **High** |
| 8 | Independent Validation Integration with Monitoring | Section V — Validation Independence | **Critical** |
| 9 | Risk-Tiered Model Inventory Linked to Monitoring | Section VI — Roles & Responsibilities | **Medium** |
| 10 | Formal Change Control for Monitoring Thresholds | Section VI — Governance & Controls | **Medium** |

---

**Compliance rating: Partial / Significant Gaps.** SOP-AIML-006 is strong on technical drift detection and operational incident response but lacks the governance depth, independence, benchmarking, process verification, and aggregate risk assessment that SR 11-7's ongoing monitoring expectations demand.

## Gap Analysis: SOP-CLIN-005 vs. NIST AI RMF MEASURE Function (including GenAI Profile)

### Overview

SOP-CLIN-005 is a mature, well-structured document with strong coverage of traditional clinical validation, calibration, and subgroup fairness analysis. However, when measured against the full NIST AI RMF MEASURE function (AI 100-1, v1.0) and the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 2024), there are **significant gaps** across multiple subcategories. Below is the detailed analysis organized by MEASURE subcategory.

---

### MEASURE 1: Appropriate Methods and Metrics

| Subcategory | Status | Gap Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **MEASURE 1.1** — Approaches and metrics for measurement of AI risks enumerated during MAP are selected; risks/trustworthiness characteristics that will not be measured are documented. | **PARTIAL** | The SOP defines metrics (ECE, AUC-ROC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV/NPV) but does **not** document which trustworthiness characteristics from the MAP function will *not* be measured. There is no explicit statement of measurement scope limitations. The GenAI Profile (MP-1.1-003) further requires documenting risk measurement plans that address cognitive biases of AI actors, known past incidents/failure modes, and over-reliance on quantitative metrics — none of which appear in the SOP. |
| **MEASURE 1.2** — Appropriateness of AI metrics and effectiveness of existing controls are regularly assessed and updated, including reports of errors and potential impacts on affected communities. | **GAP** | The SOP mandates monthly calibration audits (Section 6.2) and quarterly business reviews (Section 7.3), but there is **no process for periodically reassessing whether the metrics themselves remain appropriate**. The SOP does not require evaluating whether ECE, AUC-ROC, etc. remain the right metrics as models evolve, nor does it require incorporating error reports into metric reassessment. |
| **MEASURE 1.3** — Internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers and/or independent assessors are involved in regular assessments. Domain experts, users, AI actors external to the team, and affected communities are consulted. | **PARTIAL** | The SOP has an Independent Clinical Validation Lead and Medical Advisory Board, which partially satisfies the "independent assessor" requirement. However, there is **no mechanism for consulting affected patient communities or end-user clinicians** in the assessment process. The GenAI Profile (MP-1.2-001, MP-1.2-002) emphasizes interdisciplinary teams reflecting demographic diversity and verifying that evaluation participants are representative of diverse user populations — these are absent. |

---

### MEASURE 2: Evaluation for Trustworthy Characteristics

| Subcategory | Status | Gap Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **MEASURE 2.1** — Test sets, metrics, and details about tools used during TEVV are documented. | **PARTIAL** | The SOP documents test sets (Internal Hold-Out, Independent Validation) and metrics. However, it does **not** require documenting the specific tools (beyond naming "MLflow and LangSmith stack"), their versions, configurations, or limitations. The GenAI Profile (MS-2.13-001) specifically calls for creating measurement error models and documenting biases or statistical variance in applied metrics — entirely absent. |
| **MEASURE 2.2** — Evaluations involving human subjects meet applicable requirements (including human subject protection) and are representative of the relevant population. | **GAP** | Section 5.5 describes Human Factors evaluation in a "simulated clinical environment" but does **not** reference human subjects research requirements (IRB, informed consent, subject compensation). The GenAI Profile explicitly requires following human subjects research requirements and best practices such as informed consent and subject compensation for structured public feedback exercises. |
| **MEASURE 2.3** — AI system performance or assurance criteria are measured and demonstrated for conditions similar to deployment setting(s). | **PARTIAL** | The SOP's Silent Mode (Section 5.7) and Independent Validation Data Set from a different clinical site partially address this. However, the SOP does **not** require explicit documentation comparing test conditions to deployment conditions, nor does it address the GenAI Profile's concern about mismatches between laboratory benchmarks and real-world settings. |
| **MEASURE 2.4** — The functionality and behavior of the AI system and its components are monitored when in production. | **PARTIAL** | Section 7.1 covers real-time technical monitoring (latency, error rate, low confidence rate, data drift). However, monitoring is limited to technical KPIs — there is **no monitoring of model behavior changes** (e.g., output distribution shifts, prediction pattern changes) beyond drift scores. The GenAI Profile (MS-2.6-005) calls for verifying that system architecture can monitor outputs and performance and handle/recover from errors. |
| **MEASURE 2.5** — The AI system is demonstrated to be valid and reliable. Limitations of generalizability beyond development conditions are documented. | **PARTIAL** | The SOP requires validation against ground truth and comparison of internal vs. independent validation performance. However, there is **no explicit requirement to document limitations of generalizability** — e.g., to different patient populations, clinical settings, or equipment. The SOP's Subgroup Analysis (Section 5.8) touches on this but does not systematically address generalizability boundaries. |
| **MEASURE 2.6** — The AI system is evaluated regularly for safety risks; demonstrated to be safe; residual negative risk does not exceed risk tolerance; can fail safely, particularly beyond knowledge limits. | **PARTIAL** | The SOP has confidence thresholding (TC-02) and input validation (TC-01) as fail-safe mechanisms. However, there is **no explicit safety risk evaluation framework** beyond performance metrics. The SOP does not define "safe failure" modes, does not evaluate whether the system can fail safely when operating beyond knowledge limits, and does not document residual negative risk against organizational risk tolerance. The GenAI Profile (MS-2.6-001 through MS-2.6-007) adds requirements for assessing harmful content in training data, re-evaluating safety after fine-tuning, and reviewing outputs for validity — none of which are addressed. |
| **MEASURE 2.7** — AI system security and resilience are evaluated and documented. | **GAP** | The SOP mentions adversarial input filtering (TC-04) but provides **no security evaluation framework**. There is no requirement for penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, adversarial robustness evaluation, or resilience testing. The GenAI Profile (MS-2.7-009) requires regular assessment and verification that security measures remain effective — entirely absent. |
| **MEASURE 2.8** — Risks associated with transparency and accountability are examined and documented. | **PARTIAL** | Section 4.5 addresses transparency of outputs to clinicians. However, the SOP does **not** examine or document risks associated with transparency (e.g., over-reliance due to transparent-seeming outputs, accountability gaps in the human-AI decision chain). The GenAI Profile (MS-2.8-001 through MS-2.8-004) requires compiling statistics on policy violations, documenting data annotator instructions, using digital content transparency solutions, and verifying adequacy of user instructions — none present. |
| **MEASURE 2.9** — The AI model is explained, validated, and documented, and AI system output is interpreted within its context to inform responsible use and governance. | **PARTIAL** | The SOP requires confidence scores in natural language (Section 4.5) and validation documentation. However, there is **no requirement for model explainability techniques** (e.g., SHAP, LIME, saliency maps for imaging models). The SOP does not require documenting *how* the model arrives at predictions, only *how confident* it is. For diagnostic AI, this is a critical gap. |
| **MEASURE 2.10** — Privacy risk of the AI system is examined and documented. | **GAP** | The SOP references HIPAA-compliant audit logging (TC-05) and patient-level hashing for data splits (Section 5.2), but there is **no privacy risk examination or documentation**. No requirement for privacy impact assessment, data minimization review, membership inference attack testing, or evaluation of whether the model could leak training data. The GenAI Profile highlights data memorization and inference risks as exacerbated for generative models. |
| **MEASURE 2.11** — Fairness and bias are evaluated and results documented. | **PARTIAL** | Section 5.8 (Subgroup Analysis) is strong for demographic fairness. However, the SOP does **not** address: (a) intersectional fairness (e.g., age × ethnicity), (b) use of formal fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, equal opportunity), (c) bias in training data itself, or (d) the GenAI Profile's requirements (MS-2.11-001 through MS-2.11-004) for benchmarking systemic bias, stereotyping, denigration, and hateful content in outputs. |
| **MEASURE 2.12** — Environmental impact and sustainability of AI model training and management activities are assessed and documented. | **GAP** | **Completely absent.** The SOP has no mention of energy consumption, carbon footprint, computational resource usage, or environmental sustainability of model training or inference. The GenAI Profile specifically notes that training a single transformer LLM can emit as much carbon as 300 round-trip flights between San Francisco and New York. |
| **MEASURE 2.13** — Effectiveness of the employed TEVV metrics and processes in the MEASURE function are evaluated and documented. | **GAP** | **Completely absent.** There is no meta-evaluation of whether the measurement framework itself is effective. The GenAI Profile (MS-2.13-001) requires creating measurement error models, demonstrating construct validity for each metric, and documenting biases or statistical variance in applied metrics. |

---

### MEASURE 3: Risk Tracking Over Time

| Subcategory | Status | Gap Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **MEASURE 3.1** — Approaches, personnel, and documentation are in place to regularly identify and track existing, unanticipated, and emergent AI risks based on intended and actual performance in deployed contexts. | **PARTIAL** | The SOP has monthly post-market surveillance (Section 7.2) and quarterly business reviews (Section 7.3). However, these focus on *known* metrics (sensitivity, specificity, calibration). There is **no process for identifying emergent or unanticipated risks** — e.g., novel failure modes, unexpected clinical interactions, or new forms of bias discovered in deployment. |
| **MEASURE 3.2** — Risk tracking approaches are considered for settings where AI risks are difficult to assess using currently available measurement techniques or where metrics are not yet available. | **GAP** | **Completely absent.** The SOP assumes all risks are measurable with existing quantitative metrics. There is no acknowledgment that some risks (e.g., long-term clinical outcomes, subtle diagnostic biases, confabulation in generative diagnostic outputs) may not be capturable with current techniques. The GenAI Profile (MS-3.2-001) requires establishing processes for identifying emergent risks including consulting with external AI actors. |
| **MEASURE 3.3** — Feedback processes for end users and impacted communities to report problems and appeal system outcomes are established and integrated into AI system evaluation metrics. | **GAP** | The SOP captures clinician "AI Concordance (Agree/Disagree)" (Section 5.5) but this is a structured field, not a feedback or appeals mechanism. There is **no process for end users (clinicians) or impacted communities (patients) to report problems or appeal AI system outcomes**. The GenAI Profile (MS-3.3-001 through MS-3.3-003) requires impact assessments on how AI-generated content affects different groups, studies on how end users perceive and interact with content, and evaluation of biases in generated content using structured feedback. |

---

### MEASURE 4: Feedback About Efficacy of Measurement

| Subcategory | Status | Gap Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **MEASURE 4.1** — Measurement approaches for identifying AI risks are connected to deployment context(s) and informed through consultation with domain experts and other end users. Approaches are documented. | **GAP** | The SOP does not require connecting measurement approaches to specific deployment contexts or consulting domain experts/end users about measurement design. The Clinical Validation Lead and Medical Advisory Board provide clinical input, but this is not the same as systematically validating that measurement approaches reflect deployment realities. |
| **MEASURE 4.2** — Measurement results regarding AI system trustworthiness in deployment context(s) and across the AI lifecycle are informed by input from domain experts and relevant AI actors to validate whether the system is performing consistently as intended. | **PARTIAL** | The quarterly business review (Section 7.3) and Medical Advisory Board involvement partially address this. However, there is no structured process for domain experts and AI actors to validate that measurement results reflect consistent intended performance. |
| **MEASURE 4.3** — Measurable performance improvements or declines based on consultations with relevant AI actors, including affected communities, and field data about context-relevant risks and trustworthiness characteristics are identified and documented. | **GAP** | **Completely absent.** The SOP tracks performance trends but does not incorporate consultations with affected communities or systematically document performance improvements/declines tied to trustworthiness characteristics beyond accuracy and calibration. |

---

### GenAI Profile — Specific Gaps for Diagnostic AI

Given that SOP-CLIN-005 covers diagnostic AI systems that may incorporate generative components (e.g., LLM-based clinical decision support, generative image analysis), the following GenAI Profile-specific gaps are critical:

1. **Confabulation/Hallucination Testing (MS-2.6-004, MS-2.6-005):** No requirement to test for or monitor confabulated diagnostic outputs. For generative diagnostic AI, this is a patient-safety-critical gap.

2. **AI Red-Teaming (GenAI Profile Appendix A.1.5):** No requirement for structured red-teaming exercises to probe for flaws, vulnerabilities, harmful outputs, or jailbreaking.

6. **Measurement Error Models (MS-2.13-001):** No requirement to model or estimate biases or statistical variance in applied metrics.
